lane: I - Independent reviews, benchmarks and critiques

cards.source_title: Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Performance of Large Language Models (Tam et al., Appier / NTU)
cards.quote: Surprisingly, we observe a significant decline in LLMs reasoning abilities under format restrictions.
cards.claim: Format-restricted output (JSON-mode, JSON/XML/YAML format instructions) lowers accuracy on reasoning tasks, and stricter constraints degrade more. Classification tasks show the reverse (JSON-mode competitive). A two-step 'answer in natural language, then convert to the format' method scores close to free text. One concrete mechanism: for GPT-3.5 Turbo, JSON-mode put the 'answer' key before the 'reason' key, removing the chain-of-thought step.
cards.evidence: Authors ran gpt-3.5-turbo-0125, claude-3-haiku-20240307, gemini-1.5-flash, LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-Instruct (appendix adds Mistral-7B-v0.3 and GPT-4o-mini) on GSM8K, Last Letter, Shuffled Objects (reasoning) and DDXPlus, MultiFin, Sports Understanding, NI Task 280 (classification), mid-2024. No Claude 4+/5 model tested. Headline contested by the dottxt rebuttal (I-02) and, per the HN thread, even BoundaryML later called the paper flawed.
cards.first_guess: Land in (a) as a field-order rule for the section-5 contracts: required evidence/reasoning-style fields come before the verdict/enum field. The two-step 'reason freely, then format' shape matches an agent loop that ends with a StructuredOutput call. Treat the headline as contested, not as a rule for current models.

cards.source_title: Say What You Mean: A Response to 'Let Me Speak Freely' (.txt / dottxt blog)
cards.source_date: undated (written after the Aug 2024 paper; likely 2024)
cards.claim: The Tam et al. negative result came from unmatched prompts between conditions, a one-shot example with two names for four-name questions, an LLM 'AI parser' (claude-3-haiku) used for scoring, and conflating JSON-mode with structured generation. With like-for-like prompts, structured output scored equal or higher.
cards.evidence: Re-run by the .txt team on Llama-3-8B-Instruct only. Unstructured vs structured: GSM8K 0.77 vs 0.78, Last Letter 0.73 vs 0.77, Shuffle Object 0.41 vs 0.44. On the original Last Letter data, scorer choice alone moved results: strict regex 0.35, AI parser 0.57, flexible regex 0.61. Authors maintain the Outlines constrained-decoding library, so they have an interest; undated page; no Claude model.
cards.first_guess: Land in (b): when two brief or contract variants are compared, hold the prompt identical and score with a deterministic checker rather than an LLM judge, because the scorer alone swung results more than the treatment did. No bearing on Claude 5.x output quality.

cards.source_title: Structured outputs can hurt the performance of LLMs (Dylan Castillo, replication of the .txt rebuttal)
cards.claim: The .txt rebuttal replicates on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, but not on GPT-4o-mini: on Shuffled Objects the structured variants were much worse than unstructured. Whether structure helps or hurts depends on model and task, so it should be tested, not assumed.
cards.evidence: Independent single author (Iwana Labs) re-ran the three reasoning tasks on LLaMA3-8B-Instruct (0-shot and 3-shot) and gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18. GPT-4o-mini Shuffled Objects: unstructured 95.12 (0-shot) and 92.68 (3-shot) vs structured about 62 to 90. GSM8K about 94 vs about 93. Last Letter 3-shot: structured 94.67 vs unstructured 92.00. Small sample, one run per setting stated, no Claude model.
cards.first_guess: Supports (b): build a small A/B check (same prompt, deterministic scorer, per model) before changing how a brief forces or shapes output, instead of adopting a rule from a blog. Does not argue for or against any tool.

cards.source_title: Hacker News thread: 'Structured outputs create false confidence' (155 points, 66 comments)
cards.quote: I just changed the order of the model's properties and the problem was gone.
cards.claim: Practitioners in the thread, other than the BAML authors, said the vendor post's claim of a large accuracy loss had no concrete evals behind it and mixed schema errors with quality loss. They independently reported that property order mattered (reasoning placed after the answer gave wrong answers), that two-pass pipelines (free-form extraction, then structured formatting) worked well, and that 'CoT breaks JSON' is outdated for reasoning models that separate thinking from output.
cards.evidence: Comment threads only: hamasho (field order), Aurornis (asks for benchmarks), crystal_revenge (cites Outlines evals; suspects the post justifies BAML's parser), armcat ('feels like an advertisement'), refulgentis (CoT claim outdated), one commenter reporting 99.7% field accuracy on receipts with a two-pass design. No controlled measurements. Thread is about a BoundaryML-authored post, so the topic is vendor-seeded even though most commenters are independent.
cards.first_guess: Land in (a): confirms the field-order rule from I-01 on practitioner experience and the research-then-record split the harness already uses. Also a caution that vendor 'false confidence' claims are contested, so nothing here motivates changing current practice.

cards.source_title: Hacker News thread: 'Sampling and structured outputs in LLMs' (234 points, 92 comments)
cards.quote: If an error happens, that lets it bail out and report the problem
cards.claim: Practitioner patterns: give the schema an escape hatch so the model can report that the input does not fit rather than inventing a value (ijk); ask for reasoning first in Markdown, then a structured block parsed in code (hedgehog); constrained sampling shifts probability mass and can force a corrupt field where a parser would have caught it (hansvm); Gemini's schema path reorders fields alphabetically unless propertyOrdering is set (minimaxir). One team (hedgehog) skipped BAML as overlapping existing tooling; another commenter praised it.
cards.evidence: Comment threads only (ijk, hedgehog, hansvm, minimaxir, Jonovono, hellovai). No measurements. Gemini ordering behaviour is a user report, not checked against Google docs in this run.
cards.first_guess: Land in (a): make 'cannot determine / input does not fit' an explicit enum value or field in the section-5 contracts, so the honest-empty rule is enforced by the schema and not only by prose in the brief.

cards.source_title: BoundaryML 'SOTA function calling' post (vendor-run BFCL result) plus an independent check of the official BFCL pages
cards.quote: We did not change/fix the existing assertions (yet)
cards.claim: Headline claim that schema-aligned parsing beats native function calling, including OpenAI strict mode, on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard and is 2-4x faster, using prompting only (no JSON mode, no constrained decoding). The numbers were produced by the vendor, not by the BFCL maintainers, and the vendor's own post says they are not directly comparable to other BFCL runs.
cards.evidence: BoundaryML ran a fork of the Gorilla repo on 2024 models. Their SAP post table (n=1000 per model): gpt-4o native FC 87.4% vs SAP 93%; gpt-4o-mini 19.8% vs 92.4%; claude-3-haiku 57.3% vs 91.7%. The implausibly low native numbers suggest harness or 2024-API artefacts. Independent check: the BFCL V4 leaderboard page (updated 2026-04-12) and BFCL README do not mention BAML, and a GitHub issue search for BAML in ShishirPatil/gorilla returned 0. No independent replication found anywhere in this lane.
cards.first_guess: Do not cite the BFCL headline as evidence for this harness: it concerns 2024 models and API modes, we only use current Claude models, and no third party has reproduced it. Land in (e) as a corrected expectation.

cards.source_title: JSONSchemaBench: A Rigorous Benchmark of Structured Outputs for Language Models (Geng et al., EPFL / Microsoft / JSON Schema)
cards.quote: Constrained decoding consistently improves the performance of downstream tasks up to 4%
cards.claim: On about 10K real-world JSON Schemas, constrained decoding (Guidance best) improved downstream reasoning accuracy rather than hurting it, and OpenAI and Gemini native modes showed near-perfect compliance on the schemas they accept but very low coverage because they implement only a subset of JSON Schema.
cards.evidence: Frameworks: Guidance, Outlines, llama.cpp, XGrammar (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for quality, Llama-3.2-1B for coverage), plus OpenAI and Gemini APIs. Guidance GSM8K rose from 80.1% to 83.8%. OpenAI empirical coverage 0.30 on GitHub Easy and 0.09 on GitHub Hard. The paper says proprietary-model coverage is not comparable to the Llama numbers. Guidance, a tested engine, scored best. No Anthropic models.
cards.first_guess: Counter-evidence to 'constrained decoding hurts reasoning' for small open models, and a reminder that provider schema support is a subset. For (a), keep section-5 schemas to the plain subset (flat objects, required, enums), which the Anthropic docs also list as supported (I-14).

cards.source_title: LLMs are bad at returning code in JSON (Aider)
cards.quote: LLMs are bad at returning code in structured JSON responses.
cards.claim: Wrapping code in a JSON tool call or JSON strict mode lowered benchmark scores versus plain Markdown for every model tested. Most extra errors came from quoting and escaping, but Sonnet made no syntax errors and still scored lower, suggesting the JSON wrapper itself distracts the model. Strict mode gave no improvement over non-strict JSON.
cards.evidence: Aider's own code-editing benchmark, 133 Exercism Python exercises, 5 runs per model and strategy, on claude-3-5-sonnet-20240620, deepseek-coder V2 0724, gpt-4o-2024-05-13 and gpt-4o-2024-08-06. gpt-4o-2024-05-13 dropped only 0.4 points (within noise). Dated: these are 2024 models and a code-generation task, not a verdict-style contract.
cards.first_guess: Only relevant where a brief tempts an agent to put long text, patches or multi-line quotes inside JSON strings. Land in (a) as a rule of thumb: keep bulky artefacts in files and return paths and short quotes in the StructuredOutput payload.

cards.source_title: Bad Schemas could break your LLM Structured Outputs (Instructor project blog)
cards.quote: We need to have a systematic way of evaluating model performance
cards.claim: Field names, a reasoning field and the mode (JSON mode vs tool calling) change accuracy a lot. A single field rename took one model from 4.5% to 95%; a reasoning field raised JSON-mode accuracy from 33% to 92%; tool calling was 1-2 points better than JSON mode and far less sensitive to schema changes.
cards.evidence: Instructor contributors ran GSM8K (first 200 test questions; 50 for the reasoning-field comparison) on Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Haiku/Sonnet/Opus, GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini. Runs per setting not stated, small samples, 2024 models, and the authors maintain Instructor (interest), results not replicated.
cards.first_guess: Strongest evidence for (b) in this lane: a schema field name or description is part of the prompt, so renaming a field in a section-5 contract is a behaviour change that a hand-edited brief would never flag. Argues for a regression check on contracts, though on 2024 models.

cards.source_title: Schema-Key Wording as an Instruction Channel in Structured Generation under Constrained Decoding (Yifan Le)
cards.quote: changing only schema-key wording can substantially affect accuracy
cards.claim: Schema keys act as an implicit instruction channel: changing only their wording moves accuracy up or down depending on the model, and prompt-level and schema-level instructions interact non-additively, so tuning one can undo the other.
cards.evidence: Abstract only was read (the PDF was unreadable). Seven language models on GSM8K and Math500; effects clearer on GSM8K; the abstract gives no effect sizes. A theory condition is also offered. Constrained-decoding setting, which may not match how an agent tool validates its output.
cards.first_guess: Reinforces I-09 with a 2026 peer-reviewed source: treat contract key names as part of the brief and cover them by the same prompt regression check. Confirm effect sizes in the full paper before relying on it.

cards.source_title: The Structured Output Benchmark: A Multi-Source Benchmark for Evaluating Structured Output Quality in LLMs
cards.quote: Our results reveal a consistent pattern: models achieve near-perfect schema compliance
cards.claim: Schema validity is the easy part: models are near-perfect on schema compliance but value accuracy is much lower, so a valid structured result says little about whether its values are right. A prompt-based vs schema-constrained ablation moved JSON validity in either direction depending on the model and barely moved value accuracy.
cards.evidence: 21 models (incl. GPT-5.4, GPT-5, GPT-4.1, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-3-Flash-Preview), text 5,000 HotpotQA records, images 209, audio 115. GPT-5.4 JSON pass 99.9% on text; best value accuracy 83.0% text, 67.2% images, 23.7% audio. Audio ablation (n=115): constraints raised JSON pass for Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.860 to 0.956 but lowered GPT-5.4 0.869 to 0.808; value accuracy changed -0.007 to +0.033. Single preprint, extraction task, reasoning disabled where supported.
cards.first_guess: Land in (a) as support for the existing design: correctness of a VERDICT must come from 'path:line - quote' evidence and a fresh-context skeptic, not from the schema. No case for adding constrained decoding.

cards.source_title: Anthropic docs: Define tools - Forcing tool use
cards.quote: Forcing a tool also skips thinking on every model that accepts forced tool use
cards.claim: Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 return a 400 for tool_choice 'any' or 'tool'; manual extended thinking also rejects forced tool use; on models that accept it, a forced call skips thinking. The documented route to schema-valid JSON is tool_choice 'auto' with strict tool use, or structured outputs. The structured-outputs page adds that grammars apply to direct output but not to thinking, so the model can think freely before the constrained final answer.
cards.evidence: First-party vendor documentation, not a measurement. Independent of BAML. I did not verify how Claude Code's Workflow tool implements its StructuredOutput 'forcing', so whether this bites the harness is unknown.
cards.first_guess: Land in (a) as a check, not a change: confirm that agent() schema enforcement is tool-layer validation plus retry (which fits the docs' guidance) and not a provider-level forced tool_choice on the models the design names. Briefs should not assume a forced call leaves room for thinking.

cards.source_title: Anthropic docs: Structured outputs - refusal caveat for reasoning-style properties
cards.quote: Ask for a short explanation instead.
cards.claim: A schema property that asks for the model's thinking or step-by-step reasoning can trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal. A refusal returns HTTP 200 with stop_reason 'refusal', is billed, and the output may not match the schema. The define-tools page repeats this as 'ask for an explanation, not reasoning'. This cuts against the common advice (I-09, I-01) to add a reasoning field before the answer.
cards.evidence: First-party vendor documentation for the Messages API structured outputs and tool inputs on current Claude models. No measurement of refusal frequency. Unknown whether Workflow subagent calls surface this refusal.
cards.first_guess: Land in (a) as an audit item: grep briefs and section-5 schemas for fields named reasoning, chain_of_thought or rationale and prefer 'explanation' or 'basis'; treat a refusal stop reason as a known failure state in the honest-empty rule.

cards.source_title: Anthropic docs: Structured outputs - property order and enum casing are not fully guaranteed
cards.quote: Compare enum values case-insensitively, and avoid enum values that differ only in capitalization.
cards.claim: Even with grammar-constrained structured outputs, Claude may change the capitalisation of enum or const values (typically the first letter after a space) without any error, and required properties are emitted before optional ones regardless of schema order, so order-sensitive schemas should mark all properties required. Supported schema subset: no recursion, no min/max or length constraints, additionalProperties false, minItems 0 or 1 only.
cards.evidence: First-party vendor documentation; no measurement of how often casing drifts. Applies to Anthropic's grammar-constrained mode; not verified whether the Workflow StructuredOutput tool uses that mode or plain tool-input validation.
cards.first_guess: Land in (a): consumers of VERDICT and severity enums should normalise case, enums should differ by more than case, and the reasoning/evidence-before-verdict ordering from I-01 and I-04 needs every field required to be safe.

cards.source_title: Hacker News thread: 'Baml: The Programming Language for Agents'
cards.quote: we made it an actual turing-complete language
cards.claim: A BAML maintainer says the project began about three years ago as a DSL for structured LLM outputs and was turned into a Turing-complete language for AI workflows with testing features, claiming about 30% fewer tokens than TypeScript in some cases. Commenters questioned the need ('plain imperative programming would work') and the 'for agents' framing. This corrects the picture of BAML as only a prompt and schema DSL.
cards.evidence: Five-comment thread (8 points); maintainer aaronvg's statements in comment 48939532 and critics bediger4000 and hdjrudni. The 30% token figure is an unverified maintainer claim. No adoption data or independent evaluation of the new language.
cards.first_guess: Land in (e): by late 2026 adopting BAML would mean adopting a language and runtime, not just a schema layer, in a harness that deliberately uses plain JS Workflow scripts. This strengthens 'take ideas, do not adopt the tool' and should be checked against the BoundaryML-official lane.

notes: No independent head-to-head of schema-aligned parsing against native structured output turned up; every BAML-versus-native number traces to BoundaryML, and BAML is absent from the official BFCL page and repo. Reddit (fetch and search) and Medium (403) were blocked. WebFetch passes pages through a small model, so quotes were re-checked with copy-exact prompts. Most measurements use 2024 models. Not carded: Cognee (qualitative, small Ollama models, no data), Thoughtworks Radar (names Instructor and Pydantic AI, not BAML), grammar-aligned decoding (NeurIPS 2024), two 2026 arXiv papers on small-model and MoE constrained decoding, Future AGI (vendor, unverified).
